issues.legal_issue: An unregistered writing that merely records a previously completed family arrangement does not require registration merely because it refers to rights in immovable property, but its admission does not prove the underlying property transaction.
material_facts: The family properties had already been divided under an earlier partition, and the properties at issue had become separate properties of the family members.

The disputed family writing described adjustments said to have been made after that partition and stated that it was executed for record and remembrance; the Court found that it referred to alleged past arrangements rather than itself creating, declaring, assigning, limiting or extinguishing property rights.
The disputed receipt recorded an alleged payment connected with the respondent vacating a house portion.
The trial court allowed the writings to be marked, while the High Court held them inadmissible for want of registration and stamp duty.
issues.conclusion: The appeal was allowed and the High Court’s order was set aside. The family writing, as a record of alleged past transactions that did not itself affect property rights, could be admitted without registration; its admission did not permit the parties to prove through it a transaction affecting immovable property. On the Court’s characterization of that writing, it did not require stamp duty. The documents could be marked subject to these limitations.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 17(1)(b) and 17(1)(c) of the Registration Act, 1908, an instrument that itself operates to create, declare, assign, limit or extinguish rights in immovable property, or acknowledges consideration on account of such a transaction, is generally compulsorily registrable. Section 49(a) and (c) bars an unregistered instrument from affecting the property or being used as evidence of a transaction affecting it, while its proviso permits evidence of a collateral transaction that does not itself require a registered instrument. A family arrangement may be oral; a writing that merely records a completed arrangement is distinguishable from one that itself effects the arrangement. The Court relied on Kale v. Deputy Director of Consolidation, Subraya M.N. v. Vittala M.N., Thulasidhara v. Narayanappa, Roshan Singh v. Zile Singh, and Yellapu Uma Maheswari v. Buddha Jagadheeswararao. It also referred to Order 13 Rules 3 and 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and A.C. Lakshmipathy v. A.M. Chakrapani Reddiar on the stamp-duty treatment of a memorandum recording an existing family arrangement.

issues.definition: When a civil property proceeding concerns a writing that records a completed family arrangement after an earlier division and does not itself alter property rights, the writing may be admitted, but its admission does not prove the underlying property transaction.

issues.legal_issue: An unregistered writing may be used to evidence a collateral transaction only when that transaction does not itself require a registered instrument and using the writing does not indirectly establish a transaction affecting immovable property.
material_facts: The appellants argued that the family writing could be considered to explain the parties’ conduct and the nature of their possession, even if it could not prove the alleged relinquishment of property rights.
The respondent disputed the alleged arrangement and asserted that the appellants’ signatures had been obtained on blank papers.

The Court distinguished admitting a writing into evidence from using it as evidence of a transaction affecting property, and cautioned that a claimed collateral purpose cannot be used to circumvent the statutory bar.
issues.conclusion: A writing may be admitted for a genuine collateral purpose, including to explain conduct or possession in an appropriate case, only if that use does not establish indirectly a transaction affecting immovable property and the collateral transaction itself does not require registration. The writing cannot be used to prove an alleged property transaction that is barred from proof by its non-registration.
issues.legal_principle: The proviso to Section 49 of the Registration Act, 1908 allows an unregistered document to be received as evidence of a collateral transaction not required to be effected by registered instrument. The Court applied the distinction between a collateral transaction and the transaction affecting immovable property, relying on Muruga Mudaliar v. Subba Reddiar, N. Varada Pillai v. Jeevarathnammal, Kirpal Kaur v. Bachan Singh, K. Panchapagesa Ayyar v. K. Kalyanasundaram Ayyar, Roshan Singh v. Zile Singh, and SMS Tea Estates (P) Ltd. v. Chandmari Tea Co. Private Ltd. It emphasized that calling a purpose collateral cannot permit indirect proof of what the registration bar prohibits.
